analysis.one_liner: Gives the FTC easier procedures to write consumer-protection rules and levy fines for unfair or deceptive practices.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past a House Energy and Commerce subcommittee and died at the end of the 117th Congress without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would let the Federal Trade Commission write rules against unfair or deceptive business practices using the standard, faster rulemaking process that most federal agencies use. Today the FTC must clear higher hurdles—publishing advance notice of a rule, documenting a widespread pattern of the practice, and holding an informal hearing—before it can act. The bill would remove those hurdles, make it harder for courts to throw out FTC rules on procedural grounds, and extend civil fines to companies that violate the FTC Act itself, not just companies that violate a specific FTC rule.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers. The FTC would be able to move faster against scams, hidden fees, misleading advertising, and misuse of personal data, with the threat of civil fines applying directly to violations of the underlying law rather than only to violations of specific rules it has issued.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers facing scams and hidden fees

how_it_helps.text: The FTC could define unfair or deceptive trade practices through ordinary notice-and-comment rulemaking, without publishing advance notice of the rulemaking, finding a widespread pattern of the practice, or providing an informal hearing [S2][S3].

A court could no longer set aside an FTC rule simply because the Commission did not complete a regulatory analysis, and challenges would be judged on whether the rule is supported by substantial evidence in the rulemaking record [S2][S3].
The bill extends civil penalties to any violation of the FTC Act itself, so a company committing an unfair or deceptive practice could face fines even if no specific FTC rule covers it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Businesses that engage in unfair or deceptive practices, and firms in industries—like advertising, direct-to-consumer marketing, and data-driven tech platforms—that could face broad new FTC rules issued by majority vote and civil fines on first violations, with fewer procedural steps available to slow or block the rules in court.
analysis.who_pays_short: Firms the FTC could penalize or regulate

drawbacks.text: Removing the advance-notice requirement, the widespread-pattern finding, and the informal hearing strips procedural protections that give affected businesses a fuller chance to contest a rule before it takes effect [S2].

Extending civil penalties to violations of the FTC Act itself means a company's first violation could carry fines, since the FTC Act's standards are broad and not every violation would be preceded by a specific agency rule [S3].

Because a court could no longer set aside a rule for failure to complete a regulatory analysis, judicial review of FTC rules would be narrower, which supporters view as restoring agency power and critics view as reduced oversight [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers, the benefit is a regulator that can act more quickly against scams, hidden fees, and data misuse, with real fines behind its rules. The cost falls on businesses, which face broad fines for first violations and fewer procedural steps to contest sweeping rules. The main honest concern is design risk: the FTC Act's 'unfair or deceptive' standard is open-ended, and easier rulemaking could produce sweeping rules with less testing against evidence, even though courts could still reject rules unsupported by the rulemaking record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Consumer Protection subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Kathy Castor introduced the bill on July 16, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
Four days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Protection and Commerce, where no further action was taken for the rest of the 117th Congress [S5].
The bill had three Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support listed, and the House or Senate never voted on it [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that would have faced FTC rulemaking and civil penalties for unfair or deceptive practices are better off because the bill died; the FTC gained no new authority.

for.name: Kathy Castor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to expand FTC rulemaking and penalty authority.

against.name: Frank Pallone
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill before the full committee for a markup or sent it to the floor; it sat in subcommittee until the Congress ended.

against.name: Business and advertising industry groups
against.role: Opponents of expanded FTC rulemaking and penalty authority
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation easing FTC rulemaking and extending civil penalties to first violations of the FTC Act, arguing it exposed companies to sweeping fines and rules with reduced procedural safeguards.

sides.party_line_note: No chamber ever voted on the bill, so no roll-call picture exists; the sponsor and all three cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republicans listed in support [S4].

industries.note: The bill would let the FTC impose civil fines for unfair or deceptive practices even without a company-specific rule, and would ease the path to new advertising rules. Firms that profit from misleading claims would face faster enforcement.

With ordinary notice-and-comment rulemaking, the FTC could issue broad rules on consumer data and privacy by majority vote instead of the slower process now required. Companies monetizing personal data would face new rules and penalties.
